issues.item: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
issues.explanation: Self-blame is difficult to justify clinically here because the profile contains no Negative Appraisal items and the formulation marks Negative Appraisals as inactive with no links to other active nodes. This item introduces a strong appraisal theme that is not supported elsewhere in the selected profile.

issues.item: Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
issues.explanation: Avoiding driving or being a passenger in a vehicle is not well grounded by the rest of the profile. The memory and threat items center on sensory re-experiencing, confinement/safety, and startle, but nothing suggests a vehicle-related trauma cue. For terrorism this could occur, but in this profile it appears disconnected from the other selected items and from the inactive Triggers network.

issues.item: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
issues.explanation: Self-blame is not well supported by the rest of the profile. There are no Negative Appraisal items and no other selected items suggesting guilt, responsibility, or moral injury; for a terrorism trauma this item can occur, but here it feels clinically disconnected from the rest of the presentation.

issues.item: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: Door/window checking is a poor fit with the rest of the threat profile and trauma context. The other threat items suggest generalized hypervigilance/startle and restricted safety, but no trigger, memory, or appraisal content links the terrorism trauma to home-intrusion fear or lock-checking specifically. This makes the item feel mismatched to the formulation and selected symptoms.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategy items are not well supported by the rest of the profile. The cognitive formulation only links Memory with Maladaptive Strategies, so strategies should plausibly arise from intrusive trauma memory content. However, the selected strategies are heterogeneous and weakly connected to the memory and threat items provided.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
issues.explanation: Self-blame introduces a strong negative-appraisal theme, but no Negative Appraisals items are endorsed and that node is structurally inactive in the formulation. This makes the self-blame item stand out as clinically disconnected from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
issues.explanation: Self-blame is not inherently impossible after terrorism, but in this profile there are no Negative Appraisals items at all and the formulation specifies Negative Appraisals as inactive with no links to other nodes. A prominent self-blame strategy therefore lacks support from the rest of the profile and does not fit the stated formulation well.

issues.item: Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
issues.explanation: Avoiding driving or being a passenger in a vehicle is too specific without any corresponding trigger, memory content, or threat item tied to vehicles/transport. For a terrorism trauma this could occur, but here the rest of the profile centers on generalized hyperarousal and sensory memory rather than transport-related danger, making this item insufficiently supported and cross-node inconsistent.

issues.item: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
issues.explanation: Self-blame is clinically hard to reconcile with the rest of this profile. The other endorsed items center on sensory trauma memories and current threat/hypervigilance after terrorism, but there are no Negative Appraisal items supporting a guilt/responsibility theme, and the formulation leaves Negative Appraisals inactive. In this profile, repeated self-blame stands out as an isolated process that is not linked to the active Memory↔Threat pattern and is therefore clinically incoherent relative to the selected items and formulation.

issues.item: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategies are not well anchored to the rest of the profile. The memory and threat items describe a classic sensory re-experiencing / hypervigilance pattern after terrorism, but self-blame, avoiding driving, and avoiding conflict introduce themes that are not represented in the memory or threat content and therefore do not cohere well with the active Memory↔Threat formulation.

issues.item: Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
issues.explanation: Within Maladaptive Strategies, the selected items point in three quite different directions: moral/self-evaluative coping (self-blame), transport-specific avoidance (driving/passenger), and interpersonal avoidance (conflict). This breadth is not impossible, but here it lacks supporting trigger, appraisal, or memory content to connect them into one coherent terrorism-related syndrome.

vignette:
Vinh Trương is a 72-year-old Vietnamese American man who has spent the better part of four decades working in refugee resettlement and humanitarian aid, a vocation that grew directly from his own experience of displacement. He is married, soft-spoken, and known among colleagues for a quality of steadiness that newer staff often describe as almost preternatural. That steadiness is now fractured in ways he struggles to name, and it is what finally brought him, at his wife's gentle insistence, to a clinical intake appointment.

Fourteen months ago, Vinh was attending a community reconciliation ceremony at a civic hall in a mid-sized American city, an event organized to mark the anniversary of a Southeast Asian refugee community's arrival in the region. He had helped plan it. He was seated near the front, beside a translator he had worked with for years, when a device detonated in the lobby. The blast did not kill anyone in his immediate row, but it killed three people he could see from where he sat, including the translator beside him, and it injured dozens more. What Vinh remembers - what returns to him unbidden - is not a continuous narrative but a series of images: the ceiling tiles suspended in the air before they fell, the particular angle of light through smoke, a woman's red scarf moving as if in slow water. He remembers sound with a precision that disturbs him: a high-pitched ringing that gave way to screaming, and beneath the screaming, a low structural groan from the building itself. These images and sounds return without warning, with a vividness that carries its own cruelty, because they are also accompanied by a quality of profound unreality. He has told his wife more than once that he cannot fully accept that this happened to him - that a man who has spent his life adjacent to catastrophe should find himself inside one feels, to Vinh, like a category error. He believes, in some private and persistent way, that he should have known. He has returned to the weeks before the event hundreds of times in his mind, searching for what he missed, what he failed to read, what warning he chose not to see. He blames himself with a thoroughness that is quiet but relentless.

In the months following the attack, Vinh stopped driving. His work as a refugee aid coordinator had always required him to move between resettlement offices, community centers, and housing sites across a wide metropolitan area. He now arranges for colleagues to transport him or restructures meetings so they occur remotely, citing scheduling. His supervisor has noticed the change but has not pressed him. The practical consequence has been a slow withdrawal from the field-facing dimensions of his role - the home visits, the informal drop-ins, the relationship work that he once considered the heart of the job. He is aware of this erosion and does not know how to reverse it.

At home and at work, Vinh has become acutely attuned to his environment in ways that exhaust him. He positions himself in rooms so that he can see all exits. Ordinary sounds - a door slamming in the hallway of his office building, a car backfiring in the parking lot below - produce a full-body startle response that he finds humiliating. He has come to feel genuinely safe in only two places: his own living room and a small prayer room at his community's Buddhist temple. Everywhere else carries a low, continuous register of threat that he monitors without being able to stop. In professional settings, he has begun to avoid any exchange that might escalate into disagreement, withdrawing from advocacy conversations he would previously have led without hesitation. Colleagues have interpreted this as fatigue; Vinh knows it is something else, though he resists naming it.

What finally moved him toward help was a moment at a staff meeting when a junior colleague raised her voice in frustration - not at him, not about anything serious - and Vinh found himself unable to speak for the remainder of the hour. He drove home that evening, the first time he had been behind the wheel in months, and told his wife what had happened. She had been waiting, she said, for him to be ready. What Vinh most hopes for, sitting across from a therapist for the first time in his life, is to understand why a man who has witnessed so much can be undone by a slammed door. What he most fears is that the answer will confirm what he already suspects - that the failure, from the beginning, was his.
